en: Chapter Ten: The Correct Protocol for the Recitation of the Precepts (Part One of Four). The tenth chapter, "The Correct Protocol for the Recitation of the Precepts," concerns the *poṣadha*, which is translated as "Pure Abiding" (*jìngzhù*). The *Chūyào lǜyí* states that this is a term from the language of the kingdom of Kośala. The six-fascicle *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Poṣadha means 'nurturing' (*chángyǎng*).

It has two meanings: first, abiding in pure precepts; second, increasing merit. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* calls it *poṣadha*; if one follows the original phonetics, it is *upoṣadha*. "Upo" means "to sever" (*duàn*), and "ṣadha" means "to increase" (*zēngzhǎng*); these are merely differences in regional dialects.

It is also called "accumulation" (*caya*), "knowledge" (*jñāna*), "propriety" (*yukta*), "concord" (*sāmagrī*), "co-residence" (*sāṃvāsika*), "turning" (*pravartana*), and "permanence" (*nitya*). The *Sānqiānwēiyí* states: "Po-sa" (Uposatha) means "pure dwelling" (*viśuddhivāsa*) in the language of Qin; in its meaning, it signifies "nurturing" (*puṣṭi*) and also "harmony" (*saṃgha*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* names it the "Eight Precepts," calling them the "Uposatha vows."
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
"That which is in the mind is called 'guarding' (*saṃvara*); that which pertains to body and speech is called 'precept' (*śīla*).
The *Vinaya* says: "The method of the *poṣadha* performed in a single location is termed the 'Poṣadha-khandhaka,' which refers to the recitation of the precepts."
The ritual for the recitation of the precepts is the great framework of the Buddha-dharma;
it sustains the True and Semblance Teachings and rectifies the various dharmas of the assembly.
Yet, ordinary sentiments are easily satisfied, and their insight lacks depth and gravity.
Those who were once revered have now become base;
though one has practiced this Dharma until recently, one often gives rise to arrogance and indolence.
This is truly because, having been influenced daily and hearing it repeatedly, one follows the mind’s own superficiality and ignorance.
Judging by these circumstances, the underlying sentiment can be understood.

Formerly, King Wenxuan of Qi compiled the *Jiāzài Būsà Yí* (The Rite for Lay Upoṣadha), and the śramaṇa and bodhisattva Puzhao Da’an compiled the *Chūjiā Būsà Fǎ* (The Method for Monastic Upoṣadha); both have circulated in the world.
However, interpretations differ and mental perspectives vary;
one may simply accept and apply [the teachings], yet there is no textual basis to rely upon.
Now, I seek to follow the intent of the sūtras while consulting what I have heard.
The rough compilation is fully set forth as listed below.
However, as we live in the final age of the Semblance Dharma (*śāsanapratirūpaka*), the teachings have fallen into decline;
were it not for our mutual encouragement and support, there would ultimately be no benefit in its completion.
Therefore, I first cite exhortations and subsequently provide textual evidence.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* asks:
"How is it known that the True Dharma will endure for a long time?"
If one says that the dharma of the precepts is not destroyed, it is as stated in the *Mātṛkā*:

"Poṣadha" means the relinquishing of all evil and unwholesome dharmas, as well as the afflictions and the grasping of existence; it is so named because one realizes the white dharmas and accomplishes the ultimate practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
It is further said:
"Every half-month, one should examine oneself from the previous half-month to the current half-month: 'During this interval, have I not violated any precepts?
If there has been a violation, one should confess it before those who share the same precepts."

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "Purity" (*viśuddhi*) is the meaning of *poṣadha*. This is divided into two parts: [1] the confession of transgressions (*āpattideśanā*), and [2] the recitation of the precepts (*śīloddhāra*). Regarding the first, there are three types of purification: 1) purification through confession; 2) purification through the observance of the *poṣadha*; and 3) purification through the performance of the *pravāraṇā*. Regarding the second, there are five types of purification: 1) purification through the confession of transgressions; 2) purification through the observance of the *poṣadha*; 3) purification through the performance of the *pravāraṇā*; 4) purification through the removal of doubts; and 5) purification through the removal of remorse. Furthermore, there are seven types of purification: 1) purification through the confession of transgressions; 2) purification through the observance of the *poṣadha*; 3) purification through the performance of the *pravāraṇā*; 4) purification through the removal of doubts; 5) purification through the removal of remorse; 6) purification through the removal of latent tendencies; and 7) purification through the removal of the underlying causes. As for the third, there are six types of purification: 1) purification through the confession of transgressions; 2) purification through the observance of the *poṣadha*; 3) purification through the performance of the *pravāraṇā*; 4) purification through the removal of doubts; 5) purification through the removal of remorse; and 6) purification through the removal of both latent tendencies and their underlying causes. Among these, the first three are called "purification by means of the Dharma," while the latter four are called "purification by means of the Vinaya. Among these, the first three are called "purification by means of the Dharma," while the latter six are called "purification by means of the Vinaya. First, the *saṃgha*, and subsequently, the individual [monastic rules].
The first section is divided into four parts:
1) differences in timing; 2) miscellaneous rules and requisites; 3) the formal ritual for the recitation; and 4) a brief exposition of miscellaneous rules.
At the beginning, there are five types:
first, the three days—namely the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth—which differ from one another;
second, before and after the meal.
Third, whether by day or by night;
fourth, whether during the waxing or the waning [of the moon];
fifth, whether at the proper time or at an improper time.
The first three [cases] are from the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the observance of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is held every three days, as listed above.
It further states:
It should be recited on the *poṣadha* day.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"On the eighth and fourteenth days, the Dharma is preached; on the fifteenth day, the *poṣadha* is performed."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
It is permissible [to perform the *poṣadha*] even before the morning meal;
however, one must not perform the *poṣadha* immediately upon rising at dawn, for to do so incurs an offense.
Because later bhikṣus did not hear it,
the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"When bhikṣus who have been involved in external quarrels come [to the assembly], the Buddha permitted the recitation of the precepts to be increased or decreased."
If one knows that [the guest] will arrive on the fourteenth day, one should speak [of it] three days prior, on the thirteenth;
if he will arrive on the fifteenth day, one should speak of it on the fourteenth.
If he has already entered the boundary, one should have him bathe.
If a bhikṣu within the boundary goes outside the boundary to recite [the Prātimokṣa], and if he cannot do so, he should inform the Saṃgha, saying:
"I am unable to recite it now; I shall recite it on the fifteenth day of the latter half of the month."
Furthermore, if they still do not depart, the period is increased to fifteen days.
If they still do not depart, they are forcibly brought into harmony for the formal proclamation.
This clarifies only two stages and does not mention a third.
By the third [recitation], it must necessarily be recited together;
furthermore, there is no textual passage stating that the Dharma would perish for failing to recite it three times, yet such a false tradition has persisted for a long time.
The Vinaya states that in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, the recitation was not performed for six years.
While the Buddha still dwells in the world,
what harm is there if a single country experiences strife,
lacks peace and happiness, and fails to attain the fruits of the noble path? This is merely called the decline of the Dharma.
In the *Vinaya*, Ānanda suspected that the bhikṣu Ghoṣila had committed theft; for six *poṣadha* ceremonies, he did not participate in the communal rites with him.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If they harbor mutual resentment, they shall not recite the precepts together for twenty years."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Because the strife has persisted for a long time, the recitation of the precepts could not be performed;
now that we have briefly reached a state of harmony, it is necessary to perform the recitation at an improper time."
On whichever day a dispute is settled, on that very day it should be reconciled.
This is because the Saṃgha possesses the six harmonies: harmony in precepts, views, livelihood, body, speech, and mind.
Now, if views and precepts are not in accord, there is no meaning of the Saṃgha, because the dharma of a harmonious and pure Saṃgha cannot be established.
Second, the miscellaneous rules regarding communal requisites.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

At the time of the *poṣadha*, the assembly did not gather at the proper time, thereby obstructing the practice of the Path. The Buddha therefore established fixed times for the gathering, as previously described in the section on "Assembling the Saṃgha.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

Regarding the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*), it was because a donor asked about the number of monks in the Saṃgha but did not know it; thus, the Buddha ordered that voting sticks be distributed.
The number of śrāmaṇeras was not known, so they were counted by distributing tally-sticks (śalākā).
If someone offers items for the poṣadha ceremony, the śrāmaṇeras also receive them;
even though they do not go to the place where the poṣadha karmavācanā is performed, they do so by virtue of receiving the tally-sticks.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"In order to receive offerings, one distributes counting sticks (*śalākā*), which includes śrāmaṇeras;
even those who have not yet received the ten precepts may receive a counting stick, because they participate equally in receiving the offerings."

As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, although one who has not yet received the ten precepts is still included within the number of the Saṃgha, if it is the turn of the Saṃgha to be invited, there is no reason to exclude such a person.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"The counting sticks (*śalākā*) must be at least as short as five fingers joined together, at most as long as a single cubit (*hasta*), at most as thick as the little finger, and at least they must not be thinner than a chopstick."
If a guest arrives and it is not known [who they are], tally sticks are distributed and their number is counted.
One person distributes them and another collects them;
once the distribution is complete, they are counted.
Having counted them, he announces:
"There are so many bhikṣus, so many śrāmaṇeras, and so many persons of the renunciant community in total.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Listen to the procedure for distributing śalākās," which are here translated as "counters.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If a layperson scatters flowers upon a bhikṣu seated on a high throne, the Buddha permits it."
A bhikṣu must not accept them.
If a layperson scatters flowers that fall upon the body or robes of a bhikṣu, he should brush them away;
if they fall upon a high seat, there is no fault.
If a bhikṣu wishes to adorn the hall for the recitation of the precepts by hanging silk streamers and scattering flowers, the Buddha permits it all.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
when one intends to recite [the precepts], one should first wash one's hands clean and then take up the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
If there is fragrant liquid, it is also permissible to bathe with it.
The same applies to others who wish to take up the counting sticks (*śalākā*).
When reciting the Vinaya, because the miscellaneous and minute textual passages are difficult to keep track of, it is permitted to count them by means of the counting sticks.
First, there are five hundred [precepts], and second, seven hundred, which together comprise the *Śrāmaṇerī-śikṣāpada* for both monks and nuns.

On the day of the *poṣadha*, tasks such as sweeping the stūpas and monasteries, having others apply plaster, sprinkling the ground with fragrant water, scattering flowers and incense, and lighting lamps must all be prepared in advance; furthermore, it must be determined who shall offer prayers of blessing, recite the precepts, and distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"A junior bhikṣu should provide such items as a water jar and lamps; the senior bhikṣu (upādhyāya) should assign these duties.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
When reciting the precepts, one should recite both sections of the Vinaya;
if that is not possible, one should recite one section.
This should be recited by the senior monk (upādhyāya) or the next-ranking monk.
Regarding "non-existent," this refers to even one who can recite [the precepts].
If one explains the names of the five categories of offenses to a person who has not yet received full ordination, one incurs an offense.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, speaking thus to anyone who has committed an offense constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
When the announcement is made, one must not cover the head or the shoulders; one should remove one's leather sandals, bare the right shoulder, and distribute the counting sticks (śalākā);
those who receive the sticks should do likewise.

First, distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*) for those who have already received full ordination; after distributing the voting sticks for the novices (*śrāmaṇera*), the ritual procedure is to be proclaimed as in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
The *Pañcavargika* states:
"The Elder (*sthavira*) should recite the precepts, and the one who upholds the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) shall perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*)."

If one falls asleep on the seat for the recitation of the precepts, or folds the robes over the shoulders, or rests hands on the hips, or wears leather sandals, or lies down, or leans against something, or fails to show respect, one incurs a minor offense (duṣkṛta) in each case.
If the Elder forgets the precepts while reciting them, he should be reminded;
if he still forgets, they should be recited again;
if he forgets once more, another person should be appointed to continue the recitation in sequence, but must not repeat what has already been said.
If there are matters requiring attention that arise, the *poṣadha* will be held tomorrow.
All *karmavācanā* procedures must be performed prior to the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), for this is the method by which the Saṃgha is brought into harmony.
One should recite the precepts directly and must not do so in a chanting or melodic tone.

When the Dharma is being preached on the eighth and fourteenth days, if laypeople hear the Dharma and joyfully offer alms, these should be accepted, and the *karmadāna* (Vina) should offer a prayer of blessing.
On the fifteenth day during the *poṣadha*, a nun came to request instruction; the Elder then addressed her with words such as "Do not be negligent," as described below.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* permits reciting the precepts in a melodic chant, whereas this [practice] is prohibited in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Those who know the ritual for the *poṣadha* should all provide offerings;
otherwise, they incur an offense."
Because this person is a successor in the absence of a Buddha,
the one who recites the precepts should first recite them from memory until they are proficient, so as not to err or be confused when speaking in the midst of the Saṃgha.
Third is the formal procedure for the recitation.
Regarding the arrangement of this rite, the Vinaya does not provide full details;
therefore, contemporary practitioners generally synthesize the various schools to establish a single unified method.
Nevertheless, the specific installations performed by different lineages each vary.
Now, taking the two masters Puzhao and Dao’an as the foundation;
for the remainder, I have cited the authentic texts of the Vinaya, pruning and supplementing them to arrive at a middle path consisting of ten items.
First: the preliminary requirement of the location.
Regarding the *poṣadha* in China, there are designated *śīla-śālās* (precept halls) where one attends when the time arrives.
Here, however, there is no separate location; it is mostly held in either the lecture hall or the dining hall, and one must follow this principle accordingly.
In all cases, one sits directly upon the ground.
In China, rope beds are used, but for the most part, grass is spread upon the floor;
the reason for having a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is solely to spread it over the grass.
In this region, there were beds in ancient times;
those of the rank of Great Officer (daifu) and above would occasionally use them for comfort,
but those below that rank all sat upon mats on the floor.
After the Eastern Jin dynasty, the use of couches began to flourish.
What is currently established in monasteries mostly consists of couches and seats;
these may also be used together.
However, when practicing according to the original rules, there were many inconveniences;
therefore, the Dharma was measured according to circumstances.
Regarding the two sets of requisites:
According to the Vinaya, young bhikṣus must first prepare items such as voting counters (śalākā), lamps, water jars, and sitting mats;
as for the arrangement of flowers and incense, these should be prepared early in accordance with the previous instructions.
Third, on the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the Elder (*sthavira*) makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to inform the Saṃgha.
At present, the *karmadāna* strikes for silence and makes the announcement, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"Today is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; the community of monks is harmoniously assembled at such-and-such a place at such-and-such a time to recite the precepts and perform the *poṣadha*.
The rest is as in the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
Fourth, when the bell is struck to assemble the Sangha, it does not exclude śrāmaṇeras; all must enter the hall.
If a śrāmaṇera has a prior engagement, he must grant his consent (*chanda*) according to the Dharma, after which the counting of tally-sticks (*śalākā*) must be performed.
If there are still signs of hearing or doubt regarding the assembly, one should search throughout the entire boundary to summon them;
if no such signs exist, proceed according to the Dharma.
When the *śrāmaṇeras* and the *bhikṣusaṃgha* are to recite the precepts in two separate locations, they shall each assemble at their respective sites at the time the bell is struck.
One should recite the verse for hearing the bell.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Having subdued the enemy of Māra’s power and eliminated all fetters without remainder, the ghaṇṭā is struck in the open air; let the bhikṣus hear it and assemble."
"All you who wish to hear the Dharma and cross the ocean of birth and death, upon hearing this wondrous sound, you shall all gather here like clouds.
Next, as he entered the hall, he joined his palms with reverent composure and paid homage, reciting this verse:
"With precepts pure as the full moon, body and speech bright and stainless, when the great assembly is harmonious and free from dispute, only then can one perform the *poṣadha* together."
Having spoken thus, they each sat down in their respective positions according to seniority, with full ritual decorum as prescribed in the aforementioned *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
This is the teaching left behind by the Ultimate Teacher, the fundamental instruction for governing the Saṃgha; it is not to be compared to ordinary or other ritual matters.
Regarding the five types of offering implements:
if there are śrāmaṇeras or lay attendants, instruct them to pluck flowers;
prepare vessels for scented water, trays, stands, and bowls—using five sets or three sets of these utensils.
Intertwined with flower trays, they are arranged in rows within the hall.
If it is during the winter months when flowers are not available, one should prepare artificial flowers made of colored silk.
Spreading these materials upon the floor, they are displayed within the images.
The incense burners, counting sticks, and tables, as well as the high seat and its various appurtenances,
shall all be made solemn and upright so that they are worthy of being beheld.
Sixth, the duties of the *karmadāna* (Vina).
Three or five junior bhikṣus should assist in preparing what is required.
Each should individually cultivate dignified deportment.
The *karmadāna* takes scented water and hot water; once they have washed their hands in succession;
Carrying the warm water to the presence of the senior monk (*sthavira*), they kneel with their right knees on the ground;
having washed the senior monk’s hands, they take the counting sticks (*śalākā*) and bathe them, each reciting this verse:

“The assembly of noble Arhats and the harmonious gathering of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) bathe the pure counting sticks with fragrant water; through this *poṣadha*, may all sentient beings be delivered.”
If the senior monk is elderly or unfamiliar with current affairs, the *karmadāna* shall personally distribute the counting sticks (*śalākā*) after bathing them.
As for the remaining pure water and scented decoctions, each person shall take as much as they require, whether it be much or little.
He commanded a young bhikṣu to carry the water and walk ahead, each reciting a verse:

"The water of eight virtues purifies all dust; washing the hands removes grime so that the mind is unstained. Upholding the prohibitive precepts without transgression—may all sentient beings be likewise."
According to the ancient methods of Master Daoan, one should hold the upper part of the hand towel with the left hand and carry the lower part with the right hand as one walks.
As for the *karmadāna* holding the counting sticks and making the formal announcement, he shall have others perform this task;
the same applies to the incense water and the cleansing towels.
Furthermore, he had one person carry fragrant water and proceed, with each reciting a verse:

"Bathed and perfumed by scented water, all impurities are cleansed; the Dharma-body is complete, endowed with the five parts; Prajñā shines perfectly, fulfillment of liberation; all beings assemble together, merging in the Dharma-realm."
"These two verses were each recited upon reaching the front of the seat; they could not be spoken simultaneously.
Furthermore, regarding the two items—water and hot water—one may only wash one's hands with them; there was originally no provision for rinsing the mouth.
That such practices occur from time to time is merely the product of one's own ignorance."

Once the karmadāna has finished distributing the bathing sticks, he proceeds to the presence of the *sthavira*, stands in a place of silence, holding the stick in his left hand and the *śaṅkha* (striking mallet) in his right; the handle of the mallet must also have been purified with scented water.
The method for striking for silence is as described in the *Saṃyukta-varga*:
one should raise the hand and strike once, announcing:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"Among the assembly, who is the youngest? Let the youngest collect and protect [the tally-sticks]—this is said three times.
"Collecting" means gathering the ritual implements; "protecting" means supervising the Dharma-activities.

Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure."
Recite this three times; for others as well, it is as described above.
If two persons perform the rite face-to-face, they say only: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind," while the remaining words are the same as before.

If one has committed an offense such as a *pāyattika* or lower, regardless of whether it was raised by another or confessed by oneself, one should first perform the confession (*pratideśanā*) and then participate in the *pravāraṇā*.

If one has committed an offense such as a *sthūlātyaya* involving four or more people, it is included within the discourse on *sthūlātyaya* and even within the discourse on *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, because there is no principle of formal disciplinary punishment [for such cases].

If one follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, after the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made to suspend the ceremony, one should wait until the assembly is complete and then deal with the matter according to the Dharma; one must not obstruct the *pravāraṇā*.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:

during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), if one commits an offense and informs the Saṃgha, fearing it might hinder the recitation, one should perform a mental confession (*cittena āviṣkaraṇa*); thereafter, one is permitted to hear the precepts.
Since both are of pure conduct and their collective governance through the monastic rules is equal in efficacy, there is no hindrance to applying them accordingly.
In principle, one must record the offense committed; however, because the assembly is incomplete, it cannot yet be adjudicated, while the remainder remain pure.
In this context, if what is spoken verbally is not true, one incurs an offense; according to the transgression, it constitutes a *pāyattika*.
This differs from the case of remaining silent during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), where the offense is determined according to the specific fault incurred.
Regarding the case of a single person performing the ritual:

the Vinaya states that one should go to the place where the *poṣadha* is to be recited, sweep and sprinkle it, arrange seats, prepare water vessels, voting sticks (*śalākā*), and so forth, and wait for the visiting bhikṣus.
If there is no one present, you should go before a stupa or temple, fully assume the dignified demeanor, and with a sincere mind, speak these words aloud:
"Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu [name], am pure. (Recite this three times.)
If one commits a minor *duṣkṛta* offense, one may perform the *pravāraṇā* after confessing it through mental reflection (*cittavijñapti*).

However, if one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense intentionally or any offense more serious than that, there is no provision for punishment; yet, because such an offense must be disclosed (*vivaśana*), the rule is that one should not perform the *pravāraṇā*.
The remainder is as before.
Regarding the three great vidyās, their mixed characteristics are now questioned: Question:
Why is it that one says, "I see my transgression;
I repent," when performing *pravāraṇā* before the Saṃgha, yet says, "I am pure," during both the face-to-face (*pratimukha*) and mental (*manasikāra*) procedures?
Answer:
Within the Saṃgha, there exists the principle of formal discipline and censure, which allows for the complete fulfillment of the ritual procedures;
whereas although an individual may possess the capacity for discipline and censure, it is unable to encompass the full scope of such governance.
It is simply said that by declaring purity, one directs the mind toward the Saṃgha.
Question:
After the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) is concluded, may the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) be performed?
Answer:
According to the *Viniścaya-śāstra*, the precepts are taught first, followed by the *pravāraṇā*.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
The *pravāraṇā* is equivalent to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
Question:
May the *pravāraṇā* be performed in the presence of those who have not yet received full ordination?
Answer:
According to the Vinaya, one should perform the *karmavācanā* and the *pravāraṇā* at a place where [the person] cannot see or hear;
if they refuse to move away, the Saṃgha itself shall go to a place beyond their sight and hearing and perform them there.
In the Vinaya, it is said: "If, after an individual or the Sangha has completed the *pravāraṇā*, guests arrive—if they are few, announce purity;
if they are equal in number or more, perform the *pravāraṇā* again."
If, after two persons have performed the ritual, three more persons arrive, the Sangha performs the *pravāraṇā* according to the formal procedure;
if only two arrive, it is the same as the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) method, as previously explained.
Question:
After the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day, is it permissible to go outside the boundary?
Answer:
It is not permitted.
This is because breaking the summer retreat or being separated from one's robes occurs due to the night not yet having ended.

Even for one who has received the invitation until the fullness of the fifteenth day of the seventh month, they must likewise return to the boundary, as the ritual cannot be performed during the night.
The text says:
"And returning after seven days.
Question:
Is it permissible to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in this boundary (*sīmā*) and perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) in another place?
Answer:
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
It is not permitted; an offense is incurred.
Question:

When those who entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer retreat) have completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and received items during the summer period, may those who entered the *paścimavārṣika* (late summer retreat) receive them as well?
Answer:
When receiving items according to the monastic rules, one should ensure they are sufficient to last until the next day.
Even when distributing rooms, dwellings, or bedding, it is permitted to accept them for the sake of future needs.
Question:
Is it permissible for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) to be performed with one announcement or two announcements in the absence of difficult circumstances?
Answer:
This is not established.

In the Vinaya, regarding the six groups of bhikṣus who—first, spoke only once; second, spoke twice; spoke in whispers; spoke rapidly; did not go to the place of *pravāraṇā*; or went there but did not sit or did not speak—the Buddha ruled in each case that these were improper.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"If a young bhikṣu does not know the procedure for the *pravāraṇā*, his upādhyāya or ācārya shall instruct him;
if he still forgets or fails to remember it, the one who receives the *pravāraṇā* shall instruct him."
If one should again forget, they should recite it together, phrase by phrase.
Having been thus instructed in detail, the elder asked: "What should an older person do?
He replied:
This is also the case with the manner of young men.
Thus, in the Vinaya, when Ānanda was unable to manage the assembly, Kāśyapa rebuked him, saying he was acting like a youth;
Ānanda then said:
"My hair is now white; why then am I called 'young'?
He replied, "You have not examined the matter well; you are indeed young."
How much more so for the ignorant practitioners of old; why should they not be treated by this same principle?
Question:
Regarding the preceding and succeeding periods of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) within a boundary (*sīmā*), how is the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) conducted?
The answer says:
"From the end of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), [the monks] perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and so forth.
Question:
"Once the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has concluded, must one leave one's original location?
Answer:
The Vinaya states:
If one does not depart after the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has concluded, one commits an offense. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"Once a bhikṣu has completed the *varṣā*, he should move to another location."
If there is a valid reason and one is unable to go, there is no offense;
if there is no such reason, one may go beyond the boundary for one night and return, and there is no offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
If one does not depart after the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) has concluded, staying for even a single night constitutes an offense (*pācittiya*).
However, if no fixed invitation was made, or if it is not a place where one was invited to stay, one may remain.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
I tell you, monks: if one always dwells in a single place, there are five unrighteous things:
a longing for dwellings and utensils;
furthermore, an attachment to property out of fear that others might seize it.
Or they amass great wealth;
they are greedily attached to their kinsmen;
and they constantly associate with laypeople.
By doing the opposite of this, one obtains five merits.
Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe ritual, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vyākhyā*) translates it as "solid and firm.
It enables one to obtain many robes, and the robes will not become worn or damaged.

It is also called "Difficult to Live By," for it is difficult for the poor to find a livelihood; yet, the merit of giving even a small amount of wealth to enter this robe surpasses that of giving away the great mountain Sumeru as a garment!
Some call it "firm and solid," while others name it "sheltering cover.

In ancient translations, it was rendered as "the robe for rewarding the good and punishing the evil," intended to reward those who completed the preceding retreat; those of the subsequent retreat were not eligible to receive it.
It is also called the "Robe of Merit" (*guṇavastra*), for by the Saṃgha collectively receiving this robe, one immediately invokes five kinds of meritorious benefits.
This is divided into five parts:
first, the timing of receiving the robe.
Second, the nature and validity of the robes;
third, the distinctions regarding the persons involved;
fourth, the method for receiving the robes.
Regarding the five ways of relinquishing robes and their subsequent acquisition,
as well as the various miscellaneous characteristics that arise:
first, to clarify the time of receiving the robes.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"When the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is concluded, one should accept the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit).
Thus, those who entered the retreat early shall accept it on the sixteenth day of the seventh month and relinquish it on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month."
Therefore, the text says:
"One may relinquish [the robes] during the fourth month of winter.
In this manner, up until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one may receive the robes on every single day."
Therefore, the text says:
"Coming on that very day and not staying overnight" means that one receives the robe on the very day it is obtained; it must not remain overnight, and so forth.
Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
If it is the first day of the month, which is still the sixteenth day of the seventh month, one may receive the robe on that very day;
the same applies if it is the second or third day, up until the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"The period of receiving [the robes] is thirty days, and the period of relinquishing them is also thirty days;
thus one receives only the benefits for four months, which differs from the five-month benefits mentioned in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*."
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

"One should receive [the precepts] on the sixteenth day of the seventh month; if due to circumstances one is unable to do so, it may be done until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, but beyond this it is not permitted.
Regarding the relinquishment [of the precepts], it is likewise limited to the completion of five months, at which point they are relinquished through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*)."
Those who receive [the precepts] on the sixteenth day of the seventh month obtain the benefit for one hundred and fifty days;
those who receive them on the fifteenth day of the eighth month obtain the benefit for one hundred and twenty days;
the reductions in between may be calculated accordingly.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* asks:
"If one has received the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit) and an intercalary month occurs, how should it be treated?
It should be calculated according to the number of days of the *varṣā* retreat; thus, the intercalary month is not included in the reckoning.
Second, the explanation of the substance of the robe.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Whether one obtains a new robe, a robe offered by a donor, or a refuse-rag, a new item must be folded [and marked] to constitute its purification."
If it has already been washed, once washed, one should perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) and receive it on that very day without letting it remain overnight.

It must not have been obtained through wrong livelihood, nor obtained through deceit and crookedness, nor obtained through signs, nor obtained through incitement, and it must not be subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*).
Regarding the purification [of the robe]: it should conform to the Dharma by having a border on all four sides; a five-striped robe should have ten sections.
If the number of stripes exceeds this, one should personally wash, dye, stretch, and press it, then cut it into ten sections and sew it together.
It further states:
"One must not dye one's robes with primary colors; the use of *kāṣāya* color is permitted—this is translated here as 'non-primary color.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:

If it has not been cut or reduced in size, or if the four corners have not been folded; or if it is naturally decayed, was once a shroud for a dead person, or was brought from a cemetery—according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, "refuse" (*pāṃsukūla*) refers to that which is not the clothing of a dead person—and furthermore, if it has already been accepted as a *kaṭhina* robe, in all such cases, it does not constitute a valid robe.
However, if it is a robe made by folding layers of cloth, it is valid.
The *Mātṛkā* states:
"If a deceased bhikṣu makes use of his three robes or old garments, the acceptance is not valid;
however, if they are emergency robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) or seasonal robes (*kālāntara-cīvara*), the acceptance is valid."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"It may be made even if one has not yet used the three robes.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

If the washing, dyeing, beating, or sewing is not performed according to the Dharma; if the robe is too small or too large; if it is a garment of brocade or fine silk; if it is accepted before the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded; or if one renounces the five requirements out of greed for gain and offerings—in all such cases, the acceptance is not valid.
Conversely, if these conditions are met, the acceptance is valid.
*Samantapāsādikā*:
If it is the robe of any of the seven classes of followers, one may accept it;
if it is among the three robes, one may accept either one or two of them.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"It must have its edges bound, be provided with ties, and have hooks made; only then is it valid for acceptance.
Regarding the distinctions among the three types of persons:
First, the person who receives [the precepts] is clarified; subsequently, the person who maintains them is clarified.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"One who does not receive [the precepts] in the presence of the Saṃgha is called a person who has granted their consent (*yadṛcchā*)."
If there is an obstacle, or if one lacks the saṃghāṭī;
or if the Saṃgha has received the robe according to the Dharma, yet the person remains outside the boundary—none of these constitute [the valid distribution].
*Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*:
Those who observe the earlier *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) may receive [the offerings];
however, those who observe the later *varṣā*, those who have broken their retreat, or members of a *saṃgha* from a different boundary (*sīmā*), may not receive the benefits.
If the number of monks at this location is small and does not reach five, one may invite monks from outside the boundary to complete the quorum for receiving [the offerings].
Monks from a different boundary (sīmā) may not receive the benefits [of the robe].

If there are four bhikṣus and one śrāmaṇera at a residence, and the summer retreat is about to end, they may confer the full ordination upon the śrāmaṇera; the quorum is met, and the ordination is validly accomplished.
A newly ordained person also obtains five benefits:
one bhikṣu and four śrāmaṇeras may likewise do so because the śrāmaṇeras have fulfilled their duties during the summer retreat.

Even if there are five people residing at a location who do not understand how to receive the robes, they may invite a Sangha from another boundary who knows the Dharma to perform the *karmavācanā* and receive the robes.
Persons from different *sīmā*s cannot receive [the robe] themselves.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If various monks from different *sīmā*s wish to receive a robe but it is not possible [to do so together], they should each dissolve their original *sīmā*s, join them together to form one, and after receiving [the robe], they may subsequently re-establish their separate boundaries."
If one relinquishes [the precepts], the relinquishment is established; if one does not relinquish them, they remain dependent on the benefits [of the community].

One who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one undergoing *parivāsa*, a *śrāmaṇera* undergoing penance (*yadbhūyaskārī*), or one who has been expelled, and so forth—these do not validly receive [the precepts].
Second, regarding the person who holds the robe:

the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the custodian of the robe must possess five virtues, such as non-attachment, and must clearly and distinctly know what may be accepted and what may not be accepted.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"If many people send merit-cloths (*kaṭhina*), one should accept only one cloth; the remainder, being light items, should be divided;
heavy items belong to the Sangha of the four directions."
If the donor says, "Take these three robes and give them all," the one holding the robes shall act according to the donor's intention.

If the *karmavācanā* for the *kaṭhina* robe is performed and the robes are given to those whose robes are worn out, then if there are many whose robes are worn out, they are given to the oldest among those with worn-out robes;
if there are many who are old, they are given to the one who has spent the most summer retreats among the elders.
It must not be given to a person who is stingy or greedy.
The *Vyākhyā* on the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
At the time of first entering the retreat (*varṣā*), when one wishes to receive the *kāṭhina* robe, one must inform the Saṃgha in its entirety:
"I wish to receive this robe.
Does the Sangha consider whether this person has many distracting affairs?
Is he not likely to lose the robe?"
If this person has never been greedy for the accumulation of wealth and possesses a compassionate heart, delighting in the practice of giving, the Sangha should grant permission;
if it is not so, they need not grant it.
The fourth [section] concerns the method for receiving robes.
First is the method for making robes, followed by the explanation of the method for receiving them.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
If one obtains cloth that has not yet been made into a robe, it should be formally assigned (*karmavācanā*) among the community of monks, and a monk should be appointed to make it;
if one obtains what is already finished, it should be accepted in accordance with the Dharma.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"If the robe has not yet been completed, one should summon all the bhikṣus to help complete it.
One must not hinder the work by speaking of one's own spiritual attainments or virtues, except in the case of those who are ill."
One must not sew it together; rather, one should pierce the holes.
The reason for such earnest instruction is that this robe is praised by all Buddhas; in the past, the Tathāgata Padma was surrounded by sixteen thousand bhikṣus as they collectively fashioned it.
The various schools have extensive and clear rules regarding the making of robes; as for those existing today, most are already established, and thus they are omitted here for brevity.
Second, the clarification of formal acceptance (*sammukhīvinaya*).
One should take [the robes] and fold them crosswise, joining them at intervals of two chi; having done this five times, they should be placed in a chest before the presiding elder (*upādhyāya*).
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
"The robes should be folded and placed in a chest, with various flowers scattered upon them."
Second, the procedure for the harmonious community receiving the robes:

One should strike the bell to assemble the Sangha, then immediately exclude those who have broken their summer retreat, those who did not observe the *anvārohana* (invitation), and those who have committed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. As listed above, these individuals shall all sit separately in one place, as they are not permitted to receive the robes together;
the remainder, who are eligible to receive them, shall sit together in one place.
Although the two groups sit separately, they must follow the same communal rules; thus, they must request the consent (*chanda*) and seek harmony, responding by saying:
"The *kaṭhina* robe is being accepted through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). The presiding seat then makes the formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
Today the community of monks receives the *guṇa-vastra*.
If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:
the Saṃgha now, being in harmony, shall receive the *guṇa-vastra*.
"Thus it is announced.
Having thus made the announcement, one should ask a bhikṣu:
"Who is able to maintain the kaṭhina robe?"
The response is:
"So-and-so is able to uphold it.
The *karmavācanā* should be performed as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent:
the Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the kaṭhina robe on behalf of the Saṃgha."
The motion is thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the kaṭhina robe on behalf of the Saṃgha."
"Whichever elders consent to the Sangha appointing the bhikṣu so-and-so to hold the kaṭhina robe for the Sangha, remain silent;
whoever does not consent, speak."
The Saṃgha has consented:
the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so to hold the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha is completed.
Because the Saṃgha consents and remains silent.
"Maintain this matter thus.

He rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, knelt with his right knee on the ground before the elder, and with palms joined, addressed the one holding the robe during the *karmavācanā*: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Sangha of this residence has obtained robes that may be distributed; the present Sangha should divide them.
If the time is ripe for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen:
the Sangha shall bestow these robes upon the bhikṣu [Name]; this bhikṣu shall take these robes on behalf of the Sangha to make them into a *kaṭhina* robe, and maintain it within this residence.
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This resident Saṃgha has obtained robes that may be divided; the present Saṃgha should divide them.
The Sangha now bestows this robe upon the bhikṣu [Name]; this bhikṣu shall take this robe for the Sangha to receive and make it into a kaṭhina robe, and maintain it at this residence.

"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha holding this robe and giving it to the bhikṣu so-and-so—this bhikṣu shall take this robe and, for the sake of the Sangha, receive it as a *kaṭhina* robe to be maintained at this residence—let those who approve remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let them speak."
The Sangha has consented; this robe is given to the bhikṣu [Name] to receive and make into a *kaṭhina* robe.
The Sangha consents by its silence.
This matter is thus upheld.
He should immediately rise, take the robe-casket to the senior monk (sthavira), kneel with both knees on the ground and hold it upon his head, and then present it to the senior monk;
the senior monk shall likewise hold it upon his head.
Having repeated this three times, he placed the bundle upon the seat before the Elder;
having brushed away the flowers with his left hand, he took the edge of the robe with his right hand and held it about two feet within his left hand;
then taking another layer, and thus four layers in total, he held them together in his left hand and approached the Elder.
When the Elder saw him approaching, he immediately knelt with his legs crossed and extended his hand; the man then took the top layer of the cloth with his right hand and presented it to the Elder.
He then stepped back one layer and offered it to the second Elder;
proceeding in this manner by stepping back, he offered them all the way to the fourth Elder.
Having entrusted the robe, he returns to the lower section of the second senior monk's quarters, holding the robe in his hand and saying:
"The Sangha shall accept this robe to make it into a *kaṭhina* robe;
the Sangha now accepts this robe to make it into a *kaṭhina* robe."
"This robe has already been accepted by the community of monks as a merit-robe;
this has been stated three times. Those bhikṣus should then say:
"The one who accepted it has accepted it well."
"Whatever merit exists herein belongs to me by name.
Having each spoken thus,
they replied:
"Very well!
he should then rise and go before the fourth senior elder, take the robe in his left hand while holding it with his right hand;
having thus received it from four elders, he goes before the fifth senior elder, following the same procedure as for the first senior elder.
In this manner, having even descended from their seats, they return before the senior monk (upādhyāya), take hold of the robe, kneel with one knee on the ground toward the Saṃgha, and say:
"The Saṃgha has now reached a state of harmony and completed the acceptance of the kaṭhina robe."
5. Miscellaneous Aspects of the Relinquishment of Robes.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is permitted that [the robes] may be relinquished at the end of the four winter months; they should be brought forth [for distribution].
There are two kinds of relinquishment:
First, a bhikṣu who holds the *guṇavastuka-cīvara* (merit robe) goes beyond the boundary to stay overnight; second, the Saṃgha assembles and departs.
Furthermore, this extensively clarifies the method for losing and relinquishing through the resolution of intent (*cittotpāda*).
Now, it clarifies departing through assembly.
The Vinaya states:
"The Saṃgha has assembled;
it is in harmony."
Those who have not received the precepts should depart;
those who are absent should announce their consent (*chanda*);
the Sangha is now in harmony—what shall we do?
He replied:
"The formal ritual for the distribution of the *kaṭhina* robe.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the community of monks is bringing forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent:
the Saṃgha, being now in harmony, shall bring forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
"I declare it thus.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are several methods for relinquishing [the robe]:
if one does not relinquish it by the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, it is relinquished automatically on the sixteenth day.
The other schools enumerate eight or ten types;
each, according to how it contravenes the fundamental mind, constitutes a forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*).
Next, the five advantages (*pañca-lābha*) are explained in terms of their pervasion and obstruction.

In the Vinaya, because one has accepted this robe, [the following offenses] apply: keeping extra wealth, staying overnight apart from one's robe, declining an invitation, eating separately from the community, and visiting other households before or after the meal; each is as explained in the "Exposition of Characteristics" (Anuvyañjana).

Regarding the keeping of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), one may first receive them starting from the sixteenth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, at which time they must be formally purified (*viśuddhi*).
Other cases where "proper time" (*kāla*) and "improper time" (*akāla*) overlap are also as explained in the *Anuvyañjana* (Chapter on Characteristics).
The *Suyāma-sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva possesses four qualities by which they are free from fear and their dignified demeanor remains unshaken:
first, loss of gain; second, ill repute; third, humiliation; and fourth, suffering."
When gaining profit, the mind does not become elated; when suffering loss, the mind does not become dejected.
